ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (anterior/pos:
Overview — The “Master Gland”

The pituitary (hypophysis) sits in the sella turcica and links the brain to the endocrine system. It is really two glands of different origin fused together:

🔬 Image slot — pituitary overview — anterior (adenohypophysis) vs posterior (neurohypophysis) with the hypothalamus
Anterior (adenohypophysis)
  • Epithelial/glandular; from Rathke’s pouch (oral ectoderm); pars distalis + intermedia + tuberalis
  • Makes & secretes 6 trophic hormones under hypothalamic portal control
Posterior (neurohypophysis)
  • Neural; a downgrowth of the diencephalon (neuroectoderm); pars nervosa + infundibulum
  • Stores & releases ADH & oxytocin made in the hypothalamus
Key split: the anterior lobe synthesises its hormones (glandular); the posterior lobe only stores & releases hormones made by hypothalamic neurons (neural).
How to Recognise Each Lobe on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — anterior pituitary (cords of coloured cells + sinusoids) vs posterior (pale nervous-tissue look)
Anterior
  • Cords & clumps of epithelial cells around sinusoids
  • A mix of colours: pink (acidophils), blue/purple (basophils), pale (chromophobes)
Posterior
  • Pale, looks like nervous tissue — unmyelinated axons + glia (pituicytes)
  • Pink dilatations = Herring bodies (stored neurosecretion)
Colour is the clue: a colourful mix of cell types → anterior; a bland pale “nerve-like” field with Herring bodies → posterior.
Anterior Pituitary Cell Types
StainingCellHormone
Acidophils (pink)SomatotrophGH (growth hormone)
Lactotroph (mammotroph)Prolactin
Basophils (blue/purple)CorticotrophACTH (from POMC → also MSH, β-endorphin)

Mnemonic — basophils = “B-FLAT”: Basophils make FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH. The acidophils make GH & prolactin. Proportions: somatotrophs ~50% (most numerous), cortico-/lactotrophs ~15–20%, gonadotrophs ~10%, thyrotrophs ~5%. Agranular folliculostellate cells (S100+) support the cords. Definitive typing needs IHC.
Hypothalamo-Hypophyseal Portal System (Anterior)
🔬 Image slot — hypophyseal portal system — hypothalamic hormones via median-eminence capillaries to the anterior pituitary
  • Hypothalamic neurons release releasing/inhibiting hormones into a first capillary plexus in the median eminence.
  • The superior hypophyseal artery feeds the median-eminence primary plexus; portal veins carry hormones down the stalk to a second capillary bed bathing the anterior cells. The posterior lobe gets direct systemic blood from the inferior hypophyseal artery — so only the portal-fed anterior lobe is vulnerable in Sheehan.
Hypothalamic hormoneEffect on anterior pituitary
GHRH / somatostatin↑ / ↓ GH
TRH↑ TSH (& prolactin)
CRH↑ ACTH
GnRH↑ FSH & LH
Dopamine↓ Prolactin (tonic inhibition)
Prolactin is unique: under tonic inhibition by dopamine, so stalk damage (loss of dopamine) raises prolactin while lowering the other hormones. Primary hypothyroidism raises TRH, which also drives prolactin → hyperprolactinaemia/galactorrhoea.
Posterior Pituitary (Neurohypophysis)
🔬 Image slot — posterior pituitary — axons from hypothalamic nuclei, pituicytes and Herring bodies
  • ADH (vasopressin) — made in the supraoptic nucleus; oxytocin — made in the paraventricular nucleus (with overlap).
  • Made in hypothalamic cell bodies, transported down axons of the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract, and stored in Herring bodies until released into capillaries.
  • Pituicytes are the supporting glial cells; there is no hormone synthesis here.
ADH → V2 receptors insert aquaporin-2 (collecting-duct water) + V1 vasoconstriction; oxytocin → uterine contraction & milk let-down. Failure of ADH → diabetes insipidus; excess → SIADH.
Stains
  • H&E — separates acidophils (pink), basophils (blue/purple) & chromophobes (pale) in the anterior lobe.
  • Hormone immunohistochemistry — the definitive way to classify anterior cells & adenomas (e.g. prolactin, GH, ACTH).
  • PAS — basophil (glycoprotein-hormone) granules; useful for corticotrophs.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Prolactinoma
Commonest pituitary adenoma → galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, low libido; dopamine agonists (cabergoline). PRL >200 ng/mL = true prolactinoma; mild rise with a big tumour = stalk effect (beware the hook effect).
GH adenoma
Acromegaly (adults) / gigantism (children). Screen IGF-1; confirm failure of GH to suppress on OGTT; Rx surgery, then octreotide, pegvisomant, cabergoline.
ACTH adenoma
Cushing disease (pituitary-driven hypercortisolism)
Non-functioning adenoma
Usually gonadotroph; mass effect: bitemporal hemianopia, headache; hypopituitarism in order GH → LH/FSH → TSH → ACTH.
Sheehan syndrome
Postpartum pituitary infarction (the enlarged gland outgrows its supply) → hypopituitarism (failure to lactate)
Craniopharyngioma
Rathke’s pouch remnant; calcified suprasellar “motor-oil” cyst. Adamantinomatous (children, wet keratin) vs papillary (adults, BRAF). Vs benign Rathke cleft cyst (no calcification/keratin).
Diabetes insipidus / SIADH
Posterior-lobe/ADH disorders: too little ADH (DI, dilute urine) or too much (SIADH, dilutional hyponatraemia)
Pituitary apoplexy
Sudden haemorrhage/infarction of an adenoma → acute headache, visual loss, hypopituitarism
MEN1 & empty sella
MEN1 (3 Ps): Pituitary + Parathyroid + Pancreatic islet tumours. Empty sella: CSF-filled sella (incompetent diaphragma sellae or post-treatment); usually normal function.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Anterior = glandular (Rathke’s pouch, makes 6 hormones); posterior = neural (stores ADH & oxytocin).
Acidophils = GH & prolactin; basophils = FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH (“B-FLAT”).
Anterior pituitary is controlled by the hypophyseal portal system (two capillary beds in series).
Prolactin is tonically inhibited by dopamine → stalk section raises prolactin.
Posterior lobe: ADH (supraoptic), oxytocin (paraventricular); stored in Herring bodies; glia = pituicytes.
Prolactinoma = commonest adenoma (dopamine agonist Rx); non-functioning adenoma → bitemporal hemianopia.
Sheehan = postpartum pituitary infarction; craniopharyngioma = Rathke remnant (calcified, children).
ADH problems: too little → diabetes insipidus; too much → SIADH.
ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland:
Overview — A Gland That Stores Its Hormone Outside the Cell

The thyroid is unique: it stores hormone extracellularly as colloid inside follicles. It has two cell populations making two very different products.

🔬 Image slot — thyroid at low power — spherical follicles filled with pink colloid, lined by cuboidal cells
Follicular cells
  • Line the follicles; make T3/T4 (thyroid hormone → metabolism)
  • Endodermal origin (from the foramen caecum, descends via the thyroglossal duct; may leave a pyramidal lobe or lingual/ectopic thyroid)
C (parafollicular) cells
  • Secrete calcitonin (lowers Ca²⁺)
  • Neural-crest origin
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — thyroid follicles — cuboidal follicular epithelium, colloid, and pale parafollicular C cells
  • Spherical follicles filled with homogeneous pink colloid — the diagnostic feature.
  • Follicle wall = simple cuboidal epithelium (follicular cells) whose height reflects activity.
  • C cells — larger, pale cells singly or in small clusters, sitting on the follicular basement membrane (need immunostain to see clearly).
Active gland
  • Tall columnar follicular cells
  • Scant, scalloped colloid (resorption vacuoles)
Inactive gland
  • Flat/squamous follicular cells
  • Abundant, dense colloid
Read the cells for activity: tall cells + scalloped colloid = hyperactive (e.g. Graves); flat cells + packed colloid = inactive/colloid goitre.
Follicular Cells & Thyroid Hormone Synthesis
🔬 Image slot — thyroid hormone synthesis — iodide trapping, thyroglobulin, TPO organification, colloid resorption
1
Iodide trappingNIS (basolateral Na/I symporter, secondary active) traps iodide (~20–40× plasma)
2
Thyroglobulin + organificationIodide crosses the apex via pendrin; TPO + H₂O₂ iodinate tyrosines on thyroglobulin in the colloid
3
CouplingMIT + DIT → T3; DIT + DIT → T4 (also TPO)
4
Resorption & releaseCells endocytose colloid → lysosomes free T3/T4 into blood
T4 is the main secreted prohormone; peripheral D1/D2 convert it to active T3 (D3 makes inactive rT3). TPO is blocked by antithyroid drugs (carbimazole → methimazole; PTU also blocks D1 — preferred in the 1st trimester & thyroid storm) and by anti-TPO antibodies (Hashimoto).
C (Parafollicular) Cells
  • Neural-crest derived (via the ultimobranchial body, 4th pharyngeal pouch); lie within the follicular basement membrane but do not touch the colloid.
  • Secrete calcitonin → lowers serum Ca²⁺ by inhibiting osteoclasts (a minor role in humans, opposite of PTH).
  • Pale cytoplasm with neuroendocrine granules; stain for calcitonin & chromogranin.
C cells are the origin of medullary thyroid carcinoma (calcitonin-secreting, amyloid stroma, linked to MEN 2 / RET).
Regulation
  • TRH (hypothalamus) → TSH (pituitary) → drives follicular-cell growth & hormone synthesis/release.
  • T3/T4 negative feedback onto the pituitary & hypothalamus.
  • Chronic TSH drive (e.g. iodine deficiency) → hyperplasia & goitre.
Iodine paradoxes: a large iodide load transiently inhibits synthesis (Wolff–Chaikoff; normal glands escape in days by downregulating NIS); in a nodular gland it can instead trigger hyperthyroidism (Jod–Basedow).
Stains & Markers
  • H&E — follicles & colloid; cell height for activity.
  • PAS — colloid (glycoprotein thyroglobulin) is PAS-positive.
  • IHC: thyroglobulin is specific to follicular cells/differentiated cancer (TTF-1 is also + in medullary & lung); calcitonin, chromogranin, CEA mark C cells / medullary carcinoma (which is thyroglobulin-negative).
  • Congo red — amyloid in medullary carcinoma (apple-green birefringence).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Graves disease
TSI/TRAb (stimulating) → diffuse hyperplasia, tall cells & scalloped colloid; hyperthyroid + ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema, acropachy; Rx antithyroid drugs / radioiodine / surgery.
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Lymphocytic infiltrate + germinal centres & Hurthle cells; anti-TPO/anti-Tg; hypothyroid; risk of thyroid (MALT) lymphoma.
Multinodular / colloid goitre
Iodine deficiency/TSH drive → enlarged colloid-rich gland with nodules
Papillary carcinoma
Commonest; “Orphan-Annie” nuclei, grooves, pseudoinclusions, psammoma bodies; BRAF V600E / RET-PTC; lymphatic spread; good prognosis.
Follicular carcinoma
Diagnosed by capsular/vascular invasion (not cytology); RAS, PAX8-PPARγ; haematogenous spread (bone/lung).
Medullary carcinoma
C-cell tumour; calcitonin + amyloid; monitor calcitonin/CEA; RET: MEN2A (+phaeo/parathyroid) or MEN2B (mucosal neuromas, marfanoid, most aggressive).
Anaplastic carcinoma
Elderly; rapidly enlarging fixed mass; undifferentiated/pleomorphic (TP53); dismal prognosis.
Riedel thyroiditis
IgG4-related dense fibrosis extending beyond the capsule → hard “woody” fixed gland (mimics anaplastic).
Thyroglossal duct cyst is a midline neck swelling that moves up with tongue protrusion/swallowing — a remnant of the thyroid’s descent from the foramen caecum.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Thyroid = follicles of colloid lined by cuboidal cells; the only gland that stores hormone extracellularly.
Follicular cells make T3/T4 (metabolism); C cells make calcitonin (lowers Ca, neural-crest).
Cell height = activity: tall + scalloped colloid = active (Graves); flat + packed colloid = inactive.
Synthesis: NIS trap → TPO organification/coupling on thyroglobulin → colloid resorption → T3/T4. TPO = antithyroid-drug & Hashimoto-antibody target.
T4 = main secreted prohormone → deiodinated to active T3 peripherally.
Papillary carcinoma = commonest; Orphan-Annie nuclei, grooves, psammoma bodies; lymphatic spread.
Follicular carcinoma = capsular/vascular invasion; medullary = C cells + amyloid + calcitonin + MEN 2/RET.
Thyroglossal cyst moves with swallowing/tongue protrusion (foramen caecum remnant).
ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands:
Overview — The Calcium Guardians

Usually four (variable, ~2–6; supernumerary glands occur) tiny glands on the posterior thyroid, the parathyroids run minute-to-minute calcium control by secreting parathyroid hormone (PTH) — the dominant regulator of serum Ca²⁺.

🔬 Image slot — parathyroid at low power — cords of chief cells in a background of adipose tissue
  • Origin: superior glands from the 4th pharyngeal pouch; inferior glands from the 3rd pouch (they descend further, so ectopic/mediastinal glands are usually inferior).
  • Two cell types: chief (principal) cells (make PTH) and oxyphil cells.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — parathyroid — nests/cords of small pale chief cells with scattered eosinophilic oxyphils and fat
  • Cords & nests of small cells set in a background of mature adipose tissue (fat increases with age — up to ~50% in adults).
  • Chief cells dominate: small, uniform, round central nucleus, clear-to-pale cytoplasm (often water-clear from glycogen).
  • Oxyphil cells: fewer, larger, intensely eosinophilic (mitochondria-packed), in clusters.
Fat + two cell types = parathyroid. The intraglandular fat is the fastest way to distinguish it from thyroid (follicles) or a lymph node.
Chief Cells & PTH Secretion
  • Small principal cells with a central round nucleus and pale cytoplasm containing PTH granules. PTH is made as pre-pro-PTH → PTH (84 aa; the N-terminal 1–34 fragment is active — the basis of teriparatide).
  • They sense serum Ca²⁺ via the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR, a Gq GPCR): low Ca²⁺ → more PTH (an inverse relationship). CaSR is also in the renal TAL, where high Ca inhibits Ca reabsorption — why FHH (loss of CaSR) gives low urine Ca.
Unusual feedback: PTH is driven directly by the ion it regulates (calcium via CaSR), not by a pituitary trophic hormone.
What PTH Does — Raise Ca, Lower Phosphate
🔬 Image slot — PTH actions on bone, kidney and (via vitamin D) gut
TargetAction
Bone↑ osteoclastic resorption (indirectly, via osteoblast RANKL) → releases Ca²⁺ & phosphate
Kidney↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption (DCT); ↓ phosphate reabsorption (PCT) → phosphaturia; ↑ 1α-hydroxylase
Gut (indirect)Via activated vitamin D (calcitriol) → ↑ intestinal Ca²⁺ & phosphate absorption
Net effect: ↑ serum Ca²⁺, ↓ serum phosphate (renal phosphate wasting dominates over the phosphate released from bone/gut).
Oxyphil Cells & the Calcium Trio
Oxyphil cells
  • Appear from puberty, increase with age
  • Larger, eosinophilic, packed with mitochondria
  • Function uncertain (little PTH)
The Ca-regulating trio
  • PTH → ↑ Ca (dominant, fast)
  • Calcitriol (vit D) → ↑ gut Ca & phosphate
  • Calcitonin → ↓ Ca (minor in humans)
Stains
  • H&E — chief vs oxyphil cells against intraglandular fat.
  • PTH immunohistochemistry — confirms parathyroid tissue (vs thyroid/thymus/lymph node) and localises adenomas.
  • Intra-operative PTH assay & sestamibi scanning localise overactive glands clinically.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Primary hyperparathyroidism
Adenoma ~80–85%, hyperplasia ~10–15%, carcinoma <1% → ↑PTH, ↑Ca, ↓PO₄; “stones, bones, groans, moans”. Rx parathyroidectomy; cinacalcet (calcimimetic) if unfit.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism
CKD (↓calcitriol + hyperphosphataemia + low Ca) or vit-D deficiency → four-gland hyperplasia, ↑PTH with low/normal Ca
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism
Autonomous PTH after long-standing secondary (e.g. post-transplant) → high Ca
Hypoparathyroidism
Post-thyroidectomy (commonest), autoimmune, or DiGeorge (22q11) → low Ca, tetany (Chvostek/Trousseau), long QT. PseudohypoPTH (GNAS/Albright): high PTH but resistance → low Ca.
Osteitis fibrosa cystica
Severe hyperparathyroid bone disease → brown tumours, cysts, “salt-and-pepper” skull
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
CaSR loss-of-function (AD) → mild high Ca, low urine Ca (Ca:Cr clearance ratio <0.01); benign, do not operate.
Hypercalcaemia of malignancy
Commonest inpatient hypercalcaemia: PTHrP (squamous/renal/breast) → ↑Ca, ↓PO₄ but PTH suppressed; also osteolytic mets & myeloma. PTH-dependent (HPT/FHH) vs PTH-independent.
Parathyroid disease features in MEN 1 (parathyroid + pituitary + pancreas) and MEN 2A (parathyroid + medullary thyroid + phaeochromocytoma).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Four glands; superior = 4th pouch, inferior = 3rd pouch (inferior descends further → ectopic).
Recognise by chief cells + oxyphils in a background of fat (fat rises with age).
Chief cells make PTH; secretion is inversely driven by Ca²⁺ via the CaSR.
PTH: ↑ bone resorption (RANKL), ↑ renal Ca reabsorption, ↓ renal phosphate (phosphaturia), ↑ 1α-hydroxylase → net ↑Ca, ↓PO₄.
Oxyphil cells = larger, eosinophilic, mitochondria-rich, appear at puberty, unclear role.
Primary HPT = adenoma (high Ca); secondary = CKD/low vit D hyperplasia; tertiary = autonomous.
FHH (CaSR mutation) = high Ca + low urine Ca — do not operate.
Severe HPT bone disease = osteitis fibrosa cystica / brown tumours; MEN 1 & 2A involve parathyroids.
ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cortex/medulla:
Overview — Two Glands in One

Each adrenal (suprarenal) gland is really two endocrine organs fused together, with different embryology and products:

🔬 Image slot — adrenal gland at low power — capsule, three-zoned cortex and a central medulla
Cortex (outer)
  • Mesodermal (coelomic epithelium) origin; makes steroids from cholesterol
  • Three zones → mineralocorticoid, glucocorticoid, androgen
Medulla (central)
  • Neural-crest origin; makes catecholamines
  • Modified sympathetic tissue
How to Recognise the Regions ⭐
🔬 Image slot — adrenal cortex (pale lipid-rich zones) versus central basophilic medulla with large veins
  • Capsule of dense connective tissue on the outside.
  • Cortex — broad outer zone of pale, foamy, lipid-rich cells arranged in three patterns (see below).
  • Medulla — central, more basophilic cells in nests, with large thin-walled veins and occasional ganglion cells.
Pale lipid cortex outside, basophilic medulla inside. The abrupt change in cell colour marks the corticomedullary junction.
The Three Cortical Zones (GFR)
ZoneArchitectureProduct & control
Glomerulosa (outer)Rounded clusters/archesAldosterone — driven by angiotensin II & K⁺ (not ACTH); uniquely has aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2), lacks 17-hydroxylase (CYP17)
Fasciculata (middle, widest)Straight cords of pale “spongiocytes” (lipid-laden)Cortisol (glucocorticoid) — driven by ACTH
Reticularis (inner)Anastomosing cords, more eosinophilic (lipofuscin)Androgens (DHEA) — driven by ACTH
Mnemonic: “GFR — Salt, Sugar, Sex; the deeper you go, the sweeter it gets.” Aldosterone (salt) → cortisol (sugar) → androgens (sex). Only glomerulosa is ACTH-independent. All start from cholesterol via StAR (rate-limiting) → pregnenolone; ACTH acts via MC2R/cAMP.
The Medulla — Chromaffin Cells
🔬 Image slot — adrenal medulla — nests of chromaffin cells with a supplying vein and scattered ganglion cells
  • Chromaffin cells = modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons (neural crest) that have no axons; they secrete directly into the blood.
  • Secrete catecholamines: ~80% adrenaline + ~20% noradrenaline; the chromaffin reaction browns them with chromium salts.
  • Stimulated by preganglionic sympathetic fibres (ACh) — effectively a sympathetic ganglion without postganglionic axons.
  • PNMT (converts noradrenaline → adrenaline) requires cortisol delivered in cortical portal blood.
Markers: chromogranin A & synaptophysin (neuroendocrine); nearby sustentacular cells are S100-positive.
Blood Supply — a Cortical “Portal” to the Medulla
  • Capsular arteries feed cortical sinusoids that drain inward to the medulla — so the medulla is bathed in cortisol-rich blood.
  • This is why PNMT (and hence adrenaline synthesis) depends on the cortex.
  • A single central vein drains the gland (left → renal vein, right → IVC).
The cortex-to-medulla portal flow is a favourite exam point: destroy/suppress the cortex and adrenaline output falls because PNMT loses its cortisol.
Stains & Markers
  • H&E — pale lipid cortex vs basophilic medulla; the three cortical patterns.
  • Cortex markers: inhibin, Melan-A, SF-1, calretinin.
  • Medulla markers: chromogranin, synaptophysin; sustentacular cells S100.
  • Chromaffin reaction — chromium salts brown the catecholamine granules.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Cushing syndrome
Cortisol excess: ACTH-dependent (pituitary = Cushing disease; ectopic e.g. small-cell lung) vs ACTH-independent (adrenal adenoma/carcinoma; exogenous steroids). Central obesity, striae, myopathy; dexamethasone suppression test.
Conn syndrome
Glomerulosa aldosterone excess → hypertension + hypokalaemia, low renin (high ARR). Bilateral hyperplasia (commoner, medical) vs adenoma (surgical); Rx spironolactone.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
21-hydroxylase deficiency (~90%; ↑17-OHP) → ↓cortisol/aldosterone, ↑androgens, salt-wasting + virilisation. 11β- and 17-hydroxylase forms cause hypertension instead.
Addison disease
Primary cortical insufficiency (autoimmune in the West, TB worldwide) → fatigue, hyperpigmentation, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia; short Synacthen test; crisis → IV hydrocortisone + fluids.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen
Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage (meningococcal sepsis) → acute adrenal crisis
Phaeochromocytoma
Medullary catecholamine tumour → episodic hypertension, sweating, palpitations; “rule of 10s”; Dx metanephrines + MIBG; α-block before β-block; MEN2/VHL/NF1/SDH.
Neuroblastoma
Malignant sympathetic tumour of children; small round blue cells, Homer-Wright rosettes, urinary HVA/VMA; MYCN amplification = poor prognosis; can regress or mature to ganglioneuroma.
Adrenocortical carcinoma
Large cortical mass (functional → Cushing/virilisation, or non-functional); Weiss criteria (≥3: mitoses, necrosis, invasion…) separate it from adenoma; poor prognosis.
Nelson syndrome
After bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease, loss of feedback lets a pituitary corticotroph adenoma enlarge → mass effect + marked hyperpigmentation.
The cortex explains steroid syndromes (Cushing/Conn/CAH/Addison); the medulla explains catecholamine tumours (phaeochromocytoma, neuroblastoma).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Cortex = mesoderm/steroids; medulla = neural crest/catecholamines.
GFR = Salt, Sugar, Sex: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens).
Only zona glomerulosa is ACTH-independent (driven by angiotensin II & K⁺); it lacks 17-hydroxylase so cannot make cortisol/androgens.
Fasciculata “spongiocytes” are pale & lipid-laden (cortisol); reticularis is eosinophilic (lipofuscin, androgens).
Chromaffin cells = axon-less postganglionic sympathetic neurons; adrenaline ~80%.
Cortical portal blood delivers cortisol to the medulla → enables PNMT (NA→A).
Cortex disease: Cushing, Conn, CAH (21-hydroxylase), Addison; medulla: phaeochromocytoma, neuroblastoma.
Markers: cortex = inhibin/Melan-A/SF-1; medulla = chromogranin/synaptophysin.
ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets of Langerha:
Overview — The Endocrine Pancreas

The islets of Langerhans are ~1–2 million clusters of endocrine cells scattered through the exocrine pancreas. They are only ~1–2% of pancreatic mass but run glucose homeostasis.

🔬 Image slot — pancreas — a pale islet of Langerhans embedded among darker exocrine acini
Two pancreases in one: the exocrine acini secrete digestive enzymes into ducts; the endocrine islets secrete hormones into the blood. Islets are richest in the tail.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — islet vs acini — pale rounded islet cell cords with a rich capillary network amid eosinophilic acini
  • Pale-staining rounded clusters (“islands”) standing out against the darker, eosinophilic exocrine acini.
  • Cells in short cords/nests separated by a rich capillary network; no ducts inside.
  • The individual cell types cannot be told apart on H&E — you need immunohistochemistry.
Pale island in a pink sea = islet of Langerhans. The surrounding purple, enzyme-packed acini are the exocrine pancreas.
Islet Cell Types
Cell~%Hormone & role
Beta (β) — central~70%Insulin (+ amylin, C-peptide) → lowers glucose
Alpha (α) — peripheral~20%Glucagon → raises glucose
Delta (δ)~5–10%Somatostatin → inhibits insulin & glucagon (paracrine)
PP / F cellssmallPancreatic polypeptide → inhibits exocrine secretion & appetite
Epsilon (ε)rareGhrelin
Layout: β cells sit centrally, ringed by α and δ cells (a rodent rule; human islets are ~50–60% β, ~35% α, with cells intermingled rather than a strict core-mantle). PP/F cells cluster in the head/uncinate.
Beta Cells & Insulin Secretion
🔬 Image slot — glucose-stimulated insulin secretion — GLUT2, ATP, K_ATP closure, Ca influx, exocytosis
1
Glucose inEnters via GLUT2, phosphorylated by glucokinase (the rate-limiting glucose sensor) → glycolysis → ↑ATP
2
K⁺-ATP channel closes↑ATP shuts the channel (Kir6.2 pore + SUR1) → membrane depolarises
3
Ca²⁺ influxVoltage-gated (L-type) Ca²⁺ channels open
4
Insulin exocytosisGranules release insulin + C-peptide
  • Insulin is anabolic: ↑ glucose uptake (GLUT4 in muscle/fat), glycogenesis, lipogenesis, protein synthesis → lowers blood glucose.
  • Sulfonylureas bind SUR1 to force insulin release; C-peptide measures endogenous insulin. Incretins (GLP-1, GIP) amplify glucose-stimulated release (loss of the first-phase spike is the earliest T2DM defect).
Glucagon, Somatostatin & the Insulo-Acinar Portal System
Alpha cell / glucagon
  • Released in fasting/hypoglycaemia
  • ↑ glycogenolysis & gluconeogenesis → raises glucose
Delta cell / somatostatin
  • Paracrine brake — inhibits both insulin & glucagon
  • Also slows gut secretion/motility
Insulo-acinar portal system: islet blood drains onward to the surrounding acini, so high local insulin promotes exocrine enzyme production — linking endocrine & exocrine pancreas.
Stains & Markers
  • H&E — pale islets among darker acini.
  • Hormone IHC — insulin, glucagon, somatostatin identify cell types & islet tumours.
  • Chromogranin & synaptophysin — confirm neuroendocrine (islet) tissue.
  • Congo red — islet amyloid (IAPP) in type 2 diabetes.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Type 1 diabetes
Autoimmune β-cell destruction (T-cell insulitis; HLA-DR3/DR4; GAD/IA-2/ZnT8 antibodies) → absolute insulin deficiency; young, DKA-prone.
Type 2 diabetes
Insulin resistance + β-cell dysfunction; islet amyloid (IAPP); acute crisis = HHS. Dx HbA1c ≥6.5% / fasting ≥7.0 / OGTT ≥11.1.
Insulinoma
β-cell tumour → hypoglycaemia (Whipple’s triad); high insulin + C-peptide
Gastrinoma
Zollinger-Ellison — refractory peptic ulcers & diarrhoea
Glucagonoma
α-cell tumour → necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, weight loss
VIPoma / somatostatinoma
VIPoma → watery diarrhoea (WDHA); somatostatinoma → diabetes, gallstones, steatorrhoea
MODY
Autosomal-dominant, young, non-obese, no autoantibodies/ketosis; HNF1A (MODY3, sulfonylurea-sensitive), glucokinase (MODY2, mild stable hyperglycaemia).
Functional islet (pancreatic neuroendocrine) tumours may be part of MEN 1. Whipple’s triad for insulinoma = symptoms of hypoglycaemia + low measured glucose + relief with glucose.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Islets = pale clusters among eosinophilic acini; cell types need IHC (not H&E).
β = insulin (central, ~70%), α = glucagon (~20%), δ = somatostatin; PP & ε (ghrelin) minor.

ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland:
Overview — The Body Clock’s Gland

The pineal gland is a small cone-shaped gland in the epithalamus (roof of the third ventricle). It secretes melatonin to signal darkness and set the circadian (sleep–wake) rhythm — the “third eye.”

🔬 Image slot — pineal gland — clumps of pale pinealocytes with glial cells and calcified corpora arenacea
Derived from neuroectoderm; pinealocytes are photoreceptor-like neurons (S-antigen/arrestin +). It lacks a blood-brain barrier (fenestrated capillaries). Its famous product is melatonin; its famous landmark is calcification.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐

  • Interstitial (glial) cells — astrocyte-like supporting cells (GFAP-positive).
  • Corpora arenacea (“brain sand”) — laminated calcified concretions that increase with age — the diagnostic clue.
See laminated calcified “brain sand” among pale cell clumps → pineal gland. The calcification is a useful midline radiological landmark.
Pinealocytes & Melatonin
  • Pinealocytes synthesise melatonin: tryptophan → serotonin → (AANAT, the rate-limiting, light-suppressed enzyme) → N-acetylserotonin → (HIOMT) → melatonin. It acts on MT1/MT2 receptors.
  • Melatonin follows a strong circadian rhythm: HIGH at night / in darkness, LOW in daylight.
  • Its main job is to signal darkness and entrain the sleep–wake cycle.
Markers: pinealocytes are synaptophysin, NSE & S-antigen (arrestin) positive (a retinal photoreceptor marker); the interstitial glia are GFAP positive.

ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre:
A goitre is an enlarged thyroid — classify it by shape and function. Is it diffuse or nodular, and is the patient euthyroid, hyperthyroid or hypothyroid? Diffuse goitres are usually Graves’ disease (thyrotoxic, with eye signs and a bruit), Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (firm, often hypothyroid) or a simple / physiological goitre (see hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism). Nodular goitres are a multinodular goitre (which can become toxic) or a solitary nodule — where the job is to exclude cancer. The red flags are a hard, fixed, rapidly growing nodule with a hoarse voice or cervical lymphadenopathy (thyroid cancer), and compressive / retrosternal features (stridor, dysphagia, a positive Pemberton’s sign) (see thyroid cancer). Check thyroid function, an ultrasound, and FNA any suspicious nodule.
🚨Two goitres need urgent attention. A hard, fixed, irregular or rapidly enlarging thyroid mass — especially with a hoarse voice (recurrent laryngeal nerve), cervical lymphadenopathy or a history of neck irradiation — is thyroid cancer until an ultrasound and FNA prove otherwise (see thyroid cancer). A large or retrosternal goitre can compress the airway and vessels: look for stridor, dysphagia and a positive Pemberton’s sign (raising the arms causes facial congestion) → imaging and surgery. Remember medullary thyroid cancer can be part of MEN 2 (see multiple endocrine neoplasia), and severe thyrotoxicosis can tip into a thyroid storm (see hyperthyroidism).

ENDOCRINE__Bulging Eyes / Exophthalmos:
Exophthalmos (proptosis) is bulging of the eye — localise it by whether it is bilateral or unilateral. Bilateral proptosis is nearly always thyroid eye disease (Graves’ orbitopathy) — the commonest cause overall, with lid retraction, lid lag and injection (see hyperthyroidism, thyroid goitre). Unilateral (or markedly asymmetric) proptosis widens the differential to orbital disease: an orbital tumour or metastasis / lymphoma, orbital cellulitis (red, painful, febrile), a carotico-cavernous fistula (pulsatile, with a bruit) or cavernous sinus thrombosis (see lymphoma, cellulitis). Whatever the cause, the sight-threatening question is always the same — check visual acuity, colour vision and the pupils for optic-nerve compression, and assess for corneal exposure.
🚨Proptosis can cost the eye. Dysthyroid optic neuropathy — a crowded orbital apex compressing the optic nerve — presents with reduced acuity, colour desaturation and a relative afferent pupillary defect; it needs urgent high-dose steroids and orbital decompression (see hyperthyroidism). Orbital cellulitis — unilateral red, painful, febrile proptosis with painful / restricted eye movements — threatens sight and life → CT orbits + IV antibiotics (see cellulitis). Severe proptosis with incomplete lid closure causes exposure keratopathy → intensive lubrication. And a pulsatile proptosis with a bruit (carotico-cavernous fistula) or proptosis with fever and multiple cranial-nerve palsies (cavernous sinus thrombosis) are neurovascular emergencies.

ENDOCRINE__Weight Gain:
Weight gain is first split into true fat and fluid. Rapid weight gain with oedema is fluid — think cardiac failure (raised JVP), nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria) or liver disease (ascites) (see heart failure, nephrotic syndrome). True adiposity is usually simple energy imbalance — by far the commonest cause — but screen for the treatable endocrine causes when there are pointers: hypothyroidism (fatigue, cold, constipation), Cushing’s syndrome (central obesity, striae, proximal weakness, hypertension), and PCOS (irregular periods, hirsutism) (see hypothyroidism, Cushing’s syndrome, PCOS). Do not forget drug-induced gain (steroids, antipsychotics, insulin / sulfonylureas, some antidepressants) and depression (see depression). Obesity itself drives type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk (see type 2 diabetes).
🚨Separate fluid from fat, and don’t miss the endocrine minority. Rapid weight gain over days to weeks with oedema, breathlessness or a raised JVP is fluid overload — investigate the heart, kidneys and liver rather than the metabolism (see heart failure, nephrotic syndrome). Suspect Cushing’s syndrome when central obesity is accompanied by purple striae, proximal myopathy, easy bruising, hypertension and hyperglycaemia — and remember an exogenous cause (long-term steroids) is far commoner than an endogenous one (see Cushing’s syndrome, cushingoid habitus). Hypothyroidism causes only modest gain — large weight gain is rarely thyroid alone. And in a child, progressive obesity with hyperphagia, short stature or developmental delay suggests a hypothalamic / genetic cause.

ENDOCRINE__Heat & Cold Intolerance:
Temperature intolerance points to the thyroid first — which way is it? Heat intolerance (feeling too hot, sweaty, preferring the cold) is the hallmark of hyperthyroidism, alongside weight loss, tremor, palpitations and a goitre (see hyperthyroidism, thyroid goitre). Cold intolerance (always cold, sluggish) is the hallmark of hypothyroidism, with fatigue, weight gain and constipation (see hypothyroidism). Widen it beyond the thyroid: heat intolerance also occurs in phaeochromocytoma (episodic, with headache and hypertension), the menopause (hot flushes) and anxiety (see phaeochromocytoma, menopause). Cold intolerance also occurs in anaemia, hypopituitarism, adrenal insufficiency and a very low BMI (see anaemia, hypopituitarism). Check the thyroid function and look for the accompanying features.
🚨Two heat-intolerant states can be dangerous. Severe thyrotoxicosis can tip into a thyroid storm — fever, agitation, atrial fibrillation and heart failure — a medical emergency (see hyperthyroidism). ENDOCRINE__Excessive Sweating:
Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis) is split into focal and generalised. Primary focal hyperhidrosis — symmetrical sweating of the palms, soles and axillae from a young age, with no night sweats and no systemic upset — is benign and the commonest pattern. Generalised sweating, especially with drenching night sweats or systemic features, is secondary and needs investigation. The red flag is night sweats + weight loss + lymphadenopathy (lymphoma) or fever (TB, endocarditis) (see lymphoma, tuberculosis, infective endocarditis). Endocrine causes are common — hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma (episodic, with headache and hypertension), acromegaly, hypoglycaemia and the menopause (see hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, heat & cold intolerance). Ask about drugs, alcohol and opioid withdrawal, and anxiety.
🚨Night sweats are the symptom to fear. Drenching night sweats with weight loss and lymphadenopathy are “B symptoms” of lymphoma until proven otherwise — examine the nodes, liver and spleen (see lymphoma). They also occur in tuberculosis (cough, weight loss, travel / risk factors) and infective endocarditis (fever, a new murmur, emboli) (see tuberculosis, infective endocarditis). Phaeochromocytoma gives episodic sweating with headache, palpitations and paroxysmal hypertension and can precipitate a crisis (see phaeochromocytoma). In a person with diabetes on treatment, sweating with tremor and hunger is hypoglycaemia — check the glucose and treat immediately (see type 1 diabetes).

ENDOCRINE__Hirsutism & Virilisation:
Hirsutism is male-pattern terminal hair in a woman; virilisation is more — and the difference matters. Hirsutism (coarse hair on the face, chest and abdomen) with gradual onset and oligomenorrhoea is usually polycystic ovary syndrome — by far the commonest cause (see PCOS). Virilisation — clitoromegaly, voice deepening, male-pattern balding, increased muscle bulk, breast atrophy — means marked androgen excess, and if it comes on rapidly it is an androgen-secreting tumour (ovarian or adrenal) until proven otherwise (see gynaecological cancers). Between these sit Cushing’s syndrome (with central obesity and striae), non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (from puberty), drugs (anabolic steroids, danazol) and idiopathic / familial hirsutism (regular cycles, normal androgens) (see Cushing’s syndrome, cushingoid habitus). Measure the testosterone — a markedly raised level points to a tumour.
🚨Rapid virilisation is a tumour until proven otherwise. Rapid-onset hirsutism with virilisation (clitoromegaly, deep voice, balding, amenorrhoea) and a markedly raised testosterone points to an androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour → urgent testosterone / DHEAS and pelvic ultrasound / adrenal CT (see gynaecological cancers). Suspect Cushing’s syndrome when hirsutism accompanies central obesity, purple striae, proximal weakness, hypertension and hyperglycaemia (see Cushing’s syndrome). New hirsutism after the menopause is abnormal and warrants a tumour work-up (see menopause). And hirsutism with galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea may reflect a coexisting hyperprolactinaemia (see hyperprolactinaemia).

ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia:
Gynaecomastia is true glandular breast tissue in a male, from an imbalance of oestrogen and androgen. First separate it from pseudogynaecomastia (fatty enlargement in obesity, with no firm disc behind the nipple). Much of it is physiological — neonatal, pubertal (common and transient) and elderly (falling testosterone). Pathological causes: drugs (the commonest — spironolactone, digoxin, anti-androgens, cimetidine, cannabis, anabolic steroids), chronic liver disease and chronic kidney disease, hypogonadism (including Klinefelter’s), hyperthyroidism and hyperprolactinaemia (see liver cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, hyperprolactinaemia). Two things must not be missed: male breast cancer (a hard, eccentric, fixed lump with nipple change) and an hCG-secreting testicular tumour — so always examine the testes (see breast cancer, testicular cancer, testicular lump).
🚨Distinguish benign gynaecomastia from cancer, and always feel the testes. Male breast cancer is a hard, eccentric (not central), fixed, usually unilateral lump with nipple retraction, bleeding or skin change and axillary nodes → imaging and biopsy (see breast cancer). Rapid-onset gynaecomastia, especially with a testicular mass, suggests an hCG- or oestrogen-secreting testicular tumour — examine the testes and send hCG / AFP (see testicular cancer, testicular lump). Suspect a drug cause first in an adult (review the chart), and look for stigmata of chronic liver disease (see liver cirrhosis). Pubertal gynaecomastia is common, tender and self-limiting — reassure and review.

ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea:
Galactorrhoea is milky nipple discharge unrelated to breast-feeding — it is a sign of hyperprolactinaemia. True galactorrhoea is milky, bilateral and from multiple ducts. The first job is to separate it from pathological breast discharge — unilateral, bloody, single-duct discharge is not galactorrhoea and points to breast cancer or a papilloma (see breast cancer). Once true galactorrhoea is confirmed, find the cause of the raised prolactin: exclude pregnancy first, then drugs (dopamine antagonists — antipsychotics, metoclopramide), hypothyroidism and chronic kidney disease (see hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease). The key endocrine cause is a prolactinoma; a macroprolactinoma adds mass effect — headache, bitemporal hemianopia and hypopituitarism (see hyperprolactinaemia, bitemporal hemianopia). Check prolactin, a pregnancy test and TFTs.
🚨Two patterns change the plan. Unilateral, blood-stained, single-duct nipple discharge is not galactorrhoea — it is a breast problem (duct papilloma or carcinoma) and needs imaging and referral (see breast cancer). A very high prolactin with headache and a bitemporal visual-field defect is a macroprolactinoma compressing the optic chiasm → pituitary MRI, and it may cause hypopituitarism (see hyperprolactinaemia, bitemporal hemianopia, hypopituitarism). Always exclude pregnancy and review the drug chart (a dopamine antagonist is the commonest secondary cause). Note the “hook effect” — a huge prolactinoma can give a falsely low reading, so ask the lab to dilute if the picture fits.

1Confirm & classify
🚩Breast pathology
  • Unilateral, blood-stained, single-duct discharge = not galactorrhoea
  • Duct papilloma or carcinoma → mammography / ultrasound + referral (see breast cancer)
  • A lump, skin or nipple change raises the concern further
🚩Macroprolactinoma / pituitary mass
  • Very high prolactin + headache + bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression)
  • May cause hypopituitarism → pituitary MRI (see hyperprolactinaemia, bitemporal hemianopia, hypopituitarism)
  • Beware the “hook effect” (falsely low prolactin in huge tumours)
🟠Drug-induced
  • Dopamine antagonists: antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone; also opioids, some antidepressants
  • The commonest secondary cause — the timing follows the drug
  • Review the medication chart in every case
🟠Hypothyroidism
  • Raised TRH stimulates prolactin release → galactorrhoea
  • With cold intolerance, fatigue, weight gain — check TFTs (see hypothyroidism)
  • Correcting the thyroid normalises the prolactin
🤰Physiological / renal
  • Pregnancy and breast-feeding (exclude first), nipple stimulation, stress, chest-wall lesions
  • Chronic kidney disease (reduced prolactin clearance) (see chronic kidney disease)
  • A pregnancy test is mandatory in a woman of reproductive age
🔎Idiopathic / microprolactinoma
  • Mildly raised prolactin with a normal MRI or a small microadenoma
  • May co-secrete GH (acromegalic features) (see acromegaly)
  • Exclude macroprolactin (a biologically inactive artefact) before treating
Milky & bilateral, or bloody & unilateral? Milky, multi-duct, bilateral discharge is galactorrhoea (hyperprolactinaemia); bloody, single-duct, unilateral discharge is breast pathology. For galactorrhoea, exclude pregnancy, review drugs, check TFTs, then think prolactinoma.

The prolactin level and the MRI decide it. A very high prolactin with mass-effect symptoms is a macroprolactinoma; a modest rise is often drugs, hypothyroidism or a microadenoma. A bloody, single-duct discharge is a breast problem, not an endocrine one.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — character of the discharge, the breast, the visual fields, the drugs
History & red flags
Colour and character (milky vs bloody), unilateral vs bilateral, single vs multiple ducts, menstrual history / amenorrhoea, libido, headache and visual symptoms, a full drug history, and pregnancy risk
Examine
Confirm the discharge character and ducts; examine the breasts for a lump or skin change; check the visual fields (bitemporal hemianopia) and for features of hypothyroidism, acromegaly and hypopituitarism
Investigate
Pregnancy test, serum prolactin (fasting, rested; repeat, and request a macroprolactin screen), TFTs, U&E; a pituitary MRI if the prolactin is high or unexplained; mammography / ultrasound + biopsy for a bloody or unilateral discharge
Act
Stop / switch culprit drugs and correct hypothyroidism. Treat a prolactinoma with a dopamine agonist (cabergoline / bromocriptine) — effective even for macroadenomas, with surgery reserved for resistant / compressive cases; refer bloody / unilateral discharge to breast services
